clue.text: Nick's busy at Christmas time

parts.note: Old Nick is the Devil, but Saint Nick is the gift-bringer whose working season is Christmas

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick finds the festive season hectic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like an ordinary man, or even the Devil (Old Nick); it is Saint Nicholas, the Christmas gift-bringer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Nicholas, shortened to Nick, is the figure who delivers presents on Christmas Eve.

clue.text: Stir up a booze-up

parts.note: a rouse is an old word for a drinking bout or a full glass drunk as a toast, as in Hamlet

explanation.surface: A drinking session gets everyone excited.
explanation.walkthrough: ROUSE as a carousal is archaic (Hamlet's king 'takes his rouse'), so the booze-up is not a synonym most solvers reach first.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir up feelings or a person is to excite or awaken them, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Model thrown into part of a model for instance

definitions.text: into part of a model for instance

parts.note: a type is a model or pattern that others follow
cast means thrown, as a fishing line or dice

explanation.surface: A fashion model is pitched into some acting role.
explanation.walkthrough: An actor who is typecast is put into parts of one type over and over, a model playing models being the example offered.
explanation.definitionFit: Being typecast means being given roles of one kind repeatedly, such as an actor always playing a model.

clue.text: Slap in the face-it will stick-hence slapstick comedy

definitions.text: Slap in the face-it will stick-hence slapstick comedy

parts.words: Slap in the face-it will stick-hence slapstick comedy
parts.note: describes the gooey dessert pushed into a clown's face, which clings and gets the laugh in knockabout film comedy

explanation.surface: An explanation of where the word slapstick comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits 'slapstick' into a slap in the face and something that sticks, which is the classic thrown pudding of silent comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A creamy pudding thrown into someone's face is the stock gag of knockabout screen comedy.

clue.text: One way to facilitate inter-bank exchange in Essex

definitions.text: One way to facilitate inter-bank exchange

explanation.surface: A financial scheme for swapping money between banks, based in Essex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inter-bank exchange' suggests finance; it means crossing between riverbanks. Essex is a county just east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge lets people cross between two river banks; Abridge is also a village in the county of Essex, east of London.

clue.text: It wasn't the damned limelight Lady Macbeth objected to

definitions.text: It wasn't the damned limelight Lady Macbeth objected to

parts.words: It wasn't the damned limelight Lady Macbeth objected to
parts.note: Lady Macbeth cries 'Out, damned' mark of blood on her hand; a stage light picking out one actor has the same name

explanation.surface: Lady Macbeth was not complaining about the stage lighting.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Macbeth she sleepwalks crying 'Out, damned spot!'; the word is also a theatre spotlight, which 'limelight' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: A stain or blemish on the hand, and also a stage lamp lighting a single performer.

clue.text: Wire leg right inside?

annotationWithheld.why: Wire leg right inside? (8): LEG + R inside TEAM, where TEAM comes from 'side' within the single word 'inside', so that word is both the container indicator and the source of TEAM

clue.text: Cat with fish has ground for play

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
a tiddler is a small fish such as a stickleback

explanation.surface: A cat with a fish in its paws owns a patch of land for games.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Tiddler's ground is an old British children's game, and by extension any place where money or rewards are easily picked up.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Tiddler's ground is the playing area of a traditional chasing game, so the name stands for a play ground.

clue.text: One who made play with a sanctimonious fiddler

parts.note: pi is short for pious, meaning sanctimonious
the emperor Nero is said to have fiddled while Rome burned

explanation.surface: Someone toyed with a self-righteous violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made play' looks like teasing; it means wrote a play. Sir Arthur Wing Pinero was a Victorian playwright (The Magistrate).
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur Wing Pinero was an English dramatist, so he is one who wrote plays.

clue.text: Working in bars he takes care of many a tricky problem

definitions.text: Working in bars he takes care of many a tricky problem

parts.words: Working in bars he takes care of many a tricky problem
parts.note: bars are measures of music, and the chess problems in newspapers are set by someone of the same title

explanation.surface: A barman sorts out awkward situations for customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working in bars' suggests a pub; it is writing music in bars. Chess puzzles are also made by people with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of music works in bars, and a setter of chess problems carries the same name.

clue.text: The principal outcome

parts.note: principal here is the capital sum lent or invested, and the phrase asks what that sum earns

explanation.surface: The main result of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' reads as an adjective meaning main; it is the noun for a sum of money invested, which earns a percentage.
explanation.definitionFit: Money paid on a loan or deposit is the return that the capital sum yields.

clue.text: The Greeks' first four-in-one-letter word

parts.note: among the names of Greek letters, read in order, this is the first that has four letters; alpha before it has five

explanation.surface: A question about the earliest four-letter word in Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' tempts towards alpha, but alpha has five letters; the first four-letter name of a letter in the Greek alphabet is the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the second letter of the Greek alphabet and the first whose name runs to four letters.

clue.text: It constitutes a big danger to travellers

definitions.text: It constitutes a big danger to travellers

indicators.note: the letters of the following phrase are made up into a new word, as constituting means composing

explanation.surface: Something is a serious threat to people on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutes' rearranges A BIG DANGER, and the whole clue also describes highway robbery, the menace of travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: Highway robbery by bandits was the great peril of travellers on lonely roads.

clue.text: Officially listed, Gertie's changed colour

indicators.note: Gertie's letters are altered into a fresh order

parts.note: red is a colour

explanation.surface: Gertie's colour has been formally recorded as different.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changed' rearranges GERTIES to REGISTE, then RED follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something entered on an official record or roll has been formally recorded.

clue.text: A revolver only in case of emergency

definitions.text: A revolver only in case of emergency

parts.words: A revolver only in case of emergency
parts.note: revolver suggests a gun kept for emergencies, but here it means something that turns round, carried in the boot for a puncture

explanation.surface: Someone keeps a gun only for emergencies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' wants to be a pistol; it is anything that revolves, here the extra tyre kept for a flat.
explanation.definitionFit: The extra tyre carried in a car is only put on when one goes flat.

clue.text: Is having nothing to drink making an atom of difference?

parts.note: O is the round figure zero, meaning nothing
to tope is an old word meaning to drink heavily

explanation.surface: Staying off the drink barely makes any difference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An atom of difference' sounds like a tiny amount; it is an atom of an element that differs in neutron count.
explanation.definitionFit: Variants of one element differ only in the number of neutrons in the atom's nucleus.

clue.text: Man in possession

parts.note: possession suggests a demon or a bailiff's seizure, but here it means holding or living in a property

explanation.surface: A man who is possessed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In possession' suggests demonic possession; it means simply the one who holds or lives in a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living in or holding a house, seat or post is the one who has it.

clue.text: Creme de la cream?

parts.note: plays on creme de la creme, the best of the best, but asks which creme is the one with a cream-like custard

explanation.surface: The very best of the best.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like 'creme de la creme'; the clue wants the dessert creme ___, a set custard topped with burnt sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Creme caramel is a custard dessert, so its other word names this kind of creme.

clue.text: Sinews of war imply some harm-— amen to that!

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are taken, a run spanning the break between them

explanation.surface: Weapons are part of the harm war does, so be it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imply' is a link; 'some' takes the run across 'harm— amen to'. 'Sinews of war' is the old phrase for what war needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Weapons and military equipment are the material strength that makes waging war possible.

clue.text: Bennett character has one brief account of the heart

parts.note: The Card is Arnold Bennett's novel about the cheeky Denry Machin, a character known by that title
I is the Roman numeral one
a/c or AC is the short form of account

explanation.surface: A figure from a Bennett book has a short report on the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Bennett wrote The Card (1911), whose hero Denry is the 'card' of the title; the word also means a witty eccentric.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to the heart, as in a heart attack or a cardiac surgeon.

clue.text: "Step on it !" as the Red Queen in other words exhorted Alice

definitions.text: "Step on it !" as the Red Queen in other words exhorted Alice

parts.words: "Step on it !" as the Red Queen in other words exhorted Alice
parts.note: in Through the Looking-Glass the Red Queen drags Alice along shouting Faster! Faster!, which is the same command as step on it

explanation.surface: The Red Queen urges Alice to hurry up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass the Red Queen cries 'Faster! Faster!'; 'step on it' is slang for pressing the pedal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing the pedal to go faster is speeding up, which is what both commands demand.

clue.text: He wasn't fair to his Venetian bride

definitions.text: He wasn't fair to his Venetian bride

parts.words: He wasn't fair to his Venetian bride
parts.note: Othello, Shakespeare's dark-skinned general, smothered his Venetian wife Desdemona; fair means both just and pale-skinned

explanation.surface: A husband treated his Venetian wife unjustly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' reads as just; it also means light-skinned. Othello, Shakespeare's title character, is called 'the Moor of Venice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is a North African, the Moor of Venice, who killed Desdemona, his bride.

clue.text: What an ass to swim across the Channel with nothing on !

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece put on another sits above it, so the round letter comes first

parts.note: O is the round figure zero, meaning nothing
nager is the French verb to swim, French being the language across the English Channel

explanation.surface: Only a fool would try to swim the Channel naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across the Channel' signals French: NAGER is 'to swim'. 'With' is a link and 'on' puts O on top.
explanation.definitionFit: The onager is a wild ass of Asia, so it is one species of ass.

clue.text: What's done about the wine? It's sent out of the country

definitions.text: It's sent out of the country

indicators.note: the deed goes round the wine, which sits inside it

parts.note: a deed is a thing done, an act
port is a fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: A drinker asks what happened to the wine that was shipped abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts PORT inside DEED, splitting it DE...ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone expelled by the state to another country has been sent away by law.

clue.text: Sounds like the end of the story

indicators.note: the word for the end is said aloud and heard as a different spelling

parts.note: a tail is the hind end of an animal

explanation.surface: It sounds like the story is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end of the story' looks like a single phrase; split it, 'the end' is heard and 'story' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative or yarn told aloud or in writing is a story.

clue.text: The Ancient Mariner's emerald floaters

parts.note: in Coleridge's poem ice mast-high came floating by, as green as emerald

explanation.surface: Green objects drifting past the old sailor of the poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner has 'And ice, mast-high, came floating by, / As green as emerald.'
explanation.definitionFit: Huge masses of floating ice drifted past the Mariner's ship in the polar seas of the poem.

clue.text: We get very matey in Ealing

indicators.note: the letters of the place name are rearranged, the word in being read as in a new form

explanation.surface: People are especially friendly in the London suburb of Ealing.
explanation.walkthrough: Ealing is a district of west London. The answer is its letters rearranged, with 'in' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A friendly, warm and cheerful manner is the same as being very sociable.

clue.text: They raise tubers

parts.note: tubers sounds like root crops grown on a farm, but here it means people who ride London's Tube

explanation.surface: Farmers grow root vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tubers' wants to be potatoes and 'raise' to mean grow; tubers are users of the Tube, the London Underground, and the moving stairs lift them.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving staircases lift Underground passengers from platform to street level.
